weekLabel: Week 14 · Meeting B · Machine Learning II Studio: Classification (Track A) and Regression Refinement (Track B)

slides.title: Two tracks, one method: hand-compute your metric before you trust it.
slides.subtitle: Meeting B studio -- Track A builds a go/no-go classifier; Track B deepens Week 13's regression with compactness. Same dataset, two fitted models.
slides.teaching: Ask every student to name, out loud, which track matches their own Project 2 framing -- go/no-go or continuous outcome -- before anything runs today. Recall Monday's shared vocabulary: confusion matrix, precision/recall, threshold, cross_val_score, model card.

slides.title: Hand-compute the metric before you trust the printed number
slides.statement: Whichever track you are on, recompute your model's headline metric directly from raw counts or raw errors -- precision/recall/F1 from a confusion matrix, or the change in MAE/RMSE from Week 13's baseline -- before accepting sklearn's own printed value.
slides.supporting: Same Week 13 discipline: hand-check any metric you plan to trust.
slides.teaching: Connect explicitly back to Week 13's leakage lesson -- the habit of hand-verifying a suspiciously convenient number is the throughline across both weeks.

slides.title: meets_code, defined
slides.definition: The Track A classification TARGET: 1 if eui_kwh_m2yr <= 27.0, else 0. A design either meets this code threshold or it does not -- no partial credit, which is what makes this a CLASSIFICATION problem instead of Week 13's regression.

example.head: Class balance: realistic, not degenerate
example.body: Full n=140: 92 designs do NOT meet code, 48 do (34.3%). 'Always guess no' would already be right 65.7% of the time -- imbalanced enough to be realistic, but not so extreme the confusion matrix below becomes meaningless.

slides.note: meets_code is not a new dataset to explore -- it's a label DERIVED from eui_kwh_m2yr. Track B still predicts eui_kwh_m2yr directly; Track A predicts this yes/no label instead.
slides.teaching: Point out 34.3% out loud -- students need this number again at the AI-audit slide's naive-baseline comparison.

slides.title: [A1] Fit LogisticRegression on meets_code
slides.code:
Xc_dev, Xc_test, yc_dev, yc_test = train_test_split(
    Xc, yc, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=yc)
Xc_train, Xc_val, yc_train, yc_val = train_test_split(
    Xc_dev, yc_dev, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=yc_dev)
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(Xc_train, yc_train)
print(len(Xc_train), len(Xc_val), len(Xc_test))
print(clf.coef_.round(4))
slides.explainHead: Train learns; validation chooses; test reports
slides.explainBody: The three partitions have non-overlapping roles. Coefficients are sample-dependent associations, not proof that changing a feature causes the outcome.
slides.teaching: Order is wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc, compactness -- walk the four coefficient signs out loud against the physical story before moving on.

slides.title: [A2] Validation matrix at candidate threshold 0.5
slides.callout: Validation precision=0.857, recall=0.667, F1=0.750. Use this partition for selection; keep the final test sealed.
slides.teaching: Confusion matrix, defined -- rows are the actual class, columns are the predicted class. TN and TP are correct; FP and FN are the two DIFFERENT ways to be wrong -- a later slide argues they are not equally costly.

slides.title: Studio A1: hand-compute precision, recall, F1
slides.prompt: Validation matrix: TN=18, FP=1, FN=3, TP=6.
steps: Compute F1 from precision and recall.
slides.teaching: These are validation metrics used for policy selection—not final-test performance.

slides.title: Predict: which threshold kills false positives?
slides.kicker: Predict before you run -- Track A
slides.code:
probs_val = clf.predict_proba(Xc_val)[:, 1]
for t in [0.4, 0.5, 0.6]:
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
        yc_val, (probs_val >= t).astype(int)).ravel()
    print(t, 'FP =', fp, 'recall =', tp/(tp+fn))
slides.question: Which threshold satisfies FPR≤10% while retaining the most validation positives?
slides.why: 0.4 has FPR=2/19=10.5% and fails. Both 0.5 and 0.6 qualify, but 0.5 retains 6/9 positives versus 1/9 at 0.6.
slides.teaching: Have students commit before revealing. A common wrong guess is 0.6 because it has zero false positives, overlooking that recall collapses to 1/9. The rule selects 0.5.

slides.title: [A3] Threshold sweep: same model, only the cutoff changes
slides.teaching: As the threshold rises, precision rises and recall falls -- the standard trade-off, made concrete on one real confusion matrix instead of an abstract curve. Confirms the predict slide's answer with the full sweep.

slides.title: Choose a threshold from consequences, not a default
slides.kicker: The reasoning, not just the arithmetic

left.head: Which error is dangerous here?
left.body: A FALSE POSITIVE (model says 'meets code' when it does not) means proceeding with a design that then fails a real code review -- real rework. A FALSE NEGATIVE (model says 'no-go' when the design would have passed) just discards a viable option -- wasteful, not dangerous.

right.head: The stated rule selects threshold 0.5
right.body: Require validation FPR≤10%, then maximize recall. Threshold 0.5 qualifies with FPR=5.3% and recall=0.667. Threshold 0.6 has zero FP but recall=0.111. The chosen value equals the default by coincidence, not by unexamined convention.

slides.teaching: This is the plan's actual point -- require students to state WHY, not just report the numbers. F1 alone does not capture which error direction is dangerous.

slides.title: Studio A1's arithmetic, wrapped in a function
slides.explainHead: The three formulas you just did by hand
slides.explainBody: Nothing new is computed here -- these are exactly the three lines from Studio A1, moved inside a function so they can be run at any threshold without retyping. tn: int, fp: int, fn: int, tp: int are the type hints on the four counts; -> dict says a dictionary comes back, so the caller can reuse rates["f1"] later. Defining a function prints nothing.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment. Have students check each formula against their own Studio A1 worksheet line by line before the next slide runs it. Note the docstring + type-hint convention is required on every function they write in Project 2.

slides.title: ...continued: the same function at 0.5 and at 0.6
slides.code:
for t in [0.5, 0.6]:
    pred_t = (probs_val >= t).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(yc_val, pred_t).ravel()
    print('t =', t, tn, fp, fn, tp)
    rates_from_counts(tn, fp, fn, tp)
slides.explainBody: Both thresholds meet the FPR limit, but 0.5 retains 6 of 9 positives while 0.6 retains only 1. The predeclared rule therefore selects 0.5 on validation data.
slides.teaching: Keep probs_val and yc_val visible in the code so the final test cannot be confused with the tuning partition.

slides.title: [A4] cross_val_score: does this hold up on unseen data?
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), Xc_dev, yc_dev,
                         cv=cv, scoring='accuracy')
print(scores.round(4), round(scores.mean(), 4))
slides.explainBody: The 112 development rows are refit across paired folds. This checks default-0.5 accuracy variability; it does not validate the consequence-selected policy or touch final-test rows.
slides.teaching: Fold range is not a confidence or prediction interval.

slides.title: [A5] AI-audit: 'ready to use!'
slides.code:
def ai_evaluate_classifier(clf, X_val, y_val):
    preds = clf.predict(X_val)
    acc = (preds == y_val).mean()
    print(f'Model is {acc:.1%} accurate -- ready to use!')
    return acc
slides.output: Model is 85.7% accurate -- ready to use!
slides.explainBody: (1) One validation score is mislabeled as deployment readiness. (2) Accuracy hides the asymmetric errors. (3) No threshold rule is documented. (4) The final test has not been opened—and must remain untouched until selection is frozen.
slides.teaching: Require students to name all four defects before revealing this list -- especially #3, the naive-baseline comparison, which is easy to miss.

slides.title: [B1] Refit with compactness added
slides.code:
X_dev, X_test, y_dev, y_test = train_test_split(
    df, df['eui_kwh_m2yr'], test_size=0.20, random_state=42)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_dev, y_dev, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

lr4 = LinearRegression().fit(X_train[FEATURES4], y_train)
pred4_val = lr4.predict(X_val[FEATURES4])
print(lr4.coef_.round(4))
slides.explainHead: Fit on train; compare specifications on validation
slides.explainBody: Compactness is the candidate addition. Its fitted coefficient is an association conditional on these units and features—not a causal effect.
slides.teaching: Use the fixed 84-train / 28-validation / 28-untouched-final partition. Only the feature list changes; final-test rows remain sealed.

slides.title: [B1] continued: Week 13's helper, reused unchanged
slides.explainHead: Same function as Week 13, so the comparison is exact
slides.explainBody: The helper is unchanged, but the role is explicit: this is validation evidence used to select between 3 and 4 features. It is not final-test performance.
slides.teaching: Verify validation MAE=2.4733, RMSE=2.9129, R²=0.4258. Reusing the helper keeps the comparison fair.

slides.title: delta (the change), defined
slides.definition: The CHANGE in a metric between two model versions -- new value minus old value. Used here as delta MAE, delta RMSE, delta R2, so an improvement is stated as a number, not just a feeling that the new model is 'better.'

example.head: Track B's delta, this week
example.body: On the shared validation set: MAE falls 2.5583→2.4733 (improvement 0.0850); RMSE falls 3.0016→2.9129 (0.0888); R² rises 0.3903→0.4258 (+0.0355).

slides.note: State the subtraction convention explicitly. Here the table reports error reduction as a positive amount and R² gain as a positive amount.
slides.teaching: This delta vocabulary is what the next table's 'delta' column header actually means -- name it before the table, not after.

slides.title: [B2] Baseline vs. refined: the honest improvement
slides.callout: A modest validation gain. Confirm its direction with paired development-only folds before selecting the 4-feature specification.
slides.teaching: Connect explicitly back to Week 13's leakage lesson -- a suspiciously large jump is a red flag, not a reason to celebrate.

slides.title: Studio B1: hand-compute the improvement
steps: Explain why paired development folds are still needed before selection.
slides.teaching: The validation gain is modest. Treat it as selection evidence, not a final-test claim.

slides.title: One function, fixed train and validation rows
slides.code:
def refit_report(features: list, label: str) -> dict:
    """Fit on fixed training rows; score fixed validation rows."""
    fitted = LinearRegression().fit(
        df.loc[train_idx, features], y.loc[train_idx])
    pred = fitted.predict(df.loc[validation_idx, features])
    return report_metrics(
        y.loc[validation_idx], pred, label)
slides.explainHead: Explicit row roles prevent silent test reuse
slides.explainBody: Every feature set is fit on the same 84 training rows and scored on the same 28 validation rows. The reserved 28-row final test never enters this selection helper.
slides.teaching: The indices are fixed before comparison. Ask students to identify the only two permitted roles here: train for fitting, validation for selection.

slides.title: ...continued: both models, both deltas, one run
slides.code:
FEATURES3 = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc"]

wk13 = refit_report(FEATURES3, "3-feature")
wk14 = refit_report(FEATURES4, "4-feature")

d_mae = wk13["MAE"] - wk14["MAE"]
d_r2 = wk14["R2"] - wk13["R2"]
print("delta MAE:", round(d_mae, 4))
print("delta R2:", round(d_r2, 4))
slides.output:
3-feature validation: MAE=2.5583 RMSE=3.0016 R2=0.39029
4-feature validation: MAE=2.4733 RMSE=2.9129 R2=0.42582
delta MAE: 0.0850
delta R2: 0.0355
slides.explainBody: The validation improvement is small. The next paired cross-validation compares both feature sets on the same development folds; the untouched test still plays no role in selection.
slides.teaching: Verify the validation metrics and deltas shown here; final-test rows have not influenced the comparison.

slides.title: Predict: does cross-validation agree with the single split?
slides.kicker: Predict before you run -- Track B
slides.code:
cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
s3 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_dev[F3], y_dev, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
s4 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_dev[F4], y_dev, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
slides.question: Does the 4-feature gain recur on average across paired development folds?
options: The final test is required to answer
slides.why: Paired development folds support the direction on average: 0.2313 → 0.3225. Fold-to-fold variation remains substantial.
slides.teaching: Let students commit to an answer before revealing -- most expect 'close, but not identical,' not a negative fold. That gap is the point.

slides.title: [B3] cross_val_score: does the improvement hold up?
slides.code:
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores3 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_dev[F3], y_dev, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
scores4 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_dev[F4], y_dev, cv=cv, scoring='r2')
print(scores3.round(4), scores3.mean().round(4))
print(scores4.round(4), scores4.mean().round(4))
slides.explainHead: Paired folds support the feature choice, with variability
slides.explainBody: The 4-feature mean is higher, but scores vary across partitions. This range is not a confidence interval or an individual prediction interval.
slides.teaching: This confirms the predict slide's answer -- ask what a negative R2 means in plain language before moving to the interpretation slide.

slides.title: Paired development-fold R²
slides.callout: Select the 4-feature specification using validation plus paired development CV; then refit on all 112 development rows and open the 28-row final test once.
slides.teaching: Compare each paired fold, then the means. The fourth feature helps on average but not in every partition; that variability belongs in the model card.

slides.title: Freeze the specification before final testing
slides.kicker: The strongest argument in this block

left.head: Selection evidence
left.body: Validation R² rises 0.3903 → 0.4258; paired development-CV mean rises 0.2313 → 0.3225. Together they support the 4-feature model.

right.head: Final evidence
right.body: Refit on 112 development rows, then evaluate the untouched 28-row test once: MAE=1.9881, RMSE=2.5210, R²=0.5167.

slides.teaching: This is the sentence students should be able to say from memory before Wednesday ends -- do not let anyone round this fold up to zero or call it 'basically fine.'

slides.title: [B4] AI-audit: 'validated and ready!'
slides.code:
def ai_evaluate_regressor(model, X_test, y_test):
    r2 = model.score(X_test, y_test)
    print(f'Model explains {r2:.1%} of variance -- validated and ready!')
    return r2

ai_evaluate_regressor(lr4, X4_test, y_test4)
slides.output: Model explains 42.6% of validation variance -- validated and ready!
slides.explainBody: (1) model.score reruns the same validation split. (2) No paired model comparison. (3) No untouched final test. (4) No MAE/RMSE in physical units. (5) 'Ready' ignores extrapolation and individual uncertainty.
slides.teaching: Require at least four named defects before revealing this list -- especially #1, which students often miss because the code 'looks like' a fresh evaluation.

slides.title: Hand-computed metrics, honestly reported
takeaways: Train, validation, and final test have different roles; do not reuse the final test for threshold or feature selection.
A predeclared consequence rule—not a software default—selects Track A's threshold 0.5.
Paired development folds support Track B's 4-feature choice; final test is evaluated once after refitting.
Fold variability and test RMSE are not individual prediction intervals; state that limitation in the model card.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students state which track they are on and, in one sentence, their model card's stated limit.
